title: Machines find, people check
subtitle: Free AI bug scans for open source, an outside audit of Anthropic's risk report, and an AI-born proof that mathematicians keep shrinking
editor_note: The day's pattern: a machine turns something up, and the real work is people checking it. Anthropic's models now scan open source for vulnerabilities, but every finding needs a maintainer. METR checked Anthropic's own safety claims and found the method weaker than the verdict. An AI-generated argument about Siegel zeros went from nine pages to three as mathematicians rebuilt it. And a Reuters data story on heat storms drew a sharp statistical rebuttal within hours. This is the first issue built from a morning scan as well as your saves.

sections.headline: Anthropic will scan your open source project for bugs, free
sections.deck: OSS Scanner points Anthropic's strongest models at critical repositories on a schedule. Each finding arrives with a proof-of-concept, and often a patch.
sections.why: You ship open source agent-safety tools; this is free red-teaming, and a preview of the bug-report volume maintainers will face.

sections.headline: METR checks Anthropic's safety math and finds the method weaker than the verdict
sections.deck: It agrees catastrophic misalignment risk is low today, but doubts the report would notice if risk rose, and asks for end-to-end red-teaming of the monitors.
sections.why: The same gap shows up in agent guards: passing your own benchmark is not evidence the monitor catches what matters.

sections.quote: We’re not confident that if risk were higher, the methodology in the report would reliably identify this.

sections.headline: What agent PRs and injection evals hide

items.headline: Agent-written PRs often lose to the maintainer's own prompt
items.note: OpenCode's Dax says outside PRs come from unknown models and weaker tooling.
items.why: A useful rule for your own repos: ask contributors which model and environment produced a PR.

items.headline: Small agents ignore prompt injections more than they refuse them
items.note: Across 33,000 runs, a system prompt change moved attack success from 0.2% to 43%.
items.why: If cc-safety-net reports only attack success, a lucky ignore looks like a defense.

sections.headline: Are planet-sized heat storms new?
sections.verdict: Both agree the world is hotter. They disagree on whether heat storms are a new kind of event or the expected result of a shifted average. Read the method before the headline.
